case_study_insert.main_stem: Brackenfell Adventure Co (BAC) is a partnership in the activity tourism sector, employing a workforce of 28. Founded in 2013 by Tom and Ines Brackenfell, the business runs guided zipline, climbing and rafting trips from Bracken Gorge and uses a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. BAC plans to invest $640,000 in a new zipline and climbing centre, financed by a $400,000 bank loan and $240,000 of partners' capital. It has fixed costs of $126,000 a year, a variable cost of $18 a unit and a selling price of $33, and currently produces 14,000 units a year. BAC faces two operational problems: a skills gap among guides and seasonal labour turnover of 19% outside peak months.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — September 2026: BAC welcomed 6,800 visitors last quarter, with 3,150 zipline descents and 2,400 climbing sessions, up 18% year-on-year. Average booking lead time is 25 minutes online. Customer satisfaction averaged 4.7 out of 5 from 900 feedback forms, and complaints fell from 24 to 14 per month. A safety audit found 7 of 28 guides lack advanced swift-water rescue certification; off-the-job recertification at the regional centre costs $600 per guide and takes 2 days, while on-the-job coaching by lead guides is possible but carries no formal certification. Equipment defect rate is 0.6%.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Brackenfell Adventure Co as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, its second rise this year, increasing borrowing costs for capital projects. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.1% from $11.40 to $11.98 per hour from April 2026. (3) Fuel and transport costs have risen 10.2% year-on-year and safety-equipment prices rose 7.4%, while consumer spending on outdoor leisure grew 6.3% and domestic adventure-tourism visits are up 5.0%.

questions.question_text: BAC plans to finance the new zipline and climbing centre partly with a $400,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for BAC of using partners' capital to fund the expansion instead of a larger bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Partners' capital carries no interest or repayment obligation, protecting BAC's cash flow while the new zipline centre beds in and before revenue from the 14,000 units grows. With the base rate now at 4.75%, enlarging the $400,000 loan would add interest on top of fixed costs of $126,000 a year, squeezing the $15 contribution earned on every unit sold — partners' capital keeps the trip economics healthy from day one.

Point 2: Partners' capital keeps Tom and Ines fully in control, avoiding lender covenants that could restrict operating decisions such as seasonal opening patterns, guide ratios or the $33 pricing of zipline and climbing packages, and avoiding security over the Bracken Gorge land. It also demonstrates personal commitment from the founders, reassuring local suppliers and the regional bank on the retained $400,000 portion, protects the partnership's negotiating position, strengthens BAC's credit file for any future tranche, and keeps long-term plans for the climbing centre fully in Brackenfell hands.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development applied to BAC's financing decision and gorge operations.

questions.question_text: BAC is launching the new zipline and climbing centre. Consider a regional television and print campaign, event sponsorship at local outdoor fairs, or social media influencer marketing with adventure creators. Which should BAC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Regional television and print: Local TV and print build fast awareness across the gorge catchment and reinforce credibility for a family, safety-critical business. However, reach is expensive, audiences skew broader than adventure-seekers, and production values for outdoor products are hard to capture on a partnership budget — the spend would consume a large slice of the $640,000 investment for a 28-person business.

Event sponsorship at outdoor fairs: Sponsoring local fairs places BAC directly in front of climbers, paddlers and schools — 900 feedback forms averaging 4.7 out of 5 show that in-person endorsement works for BAC. Sponsorship is tangible and credibility-building (demo days, helmets, taster descents) but limited to fair dates, seasonal, and local in reach; it cannot scale or sustain off-peak bookings across the shoulder months when turnover hits 19%.

Social media influencer marketing: Adventure creators filming zipline descents, climbing sessions and rafting runs reach exactly the outdoor-leisure audience growing 6.3% and the domestic adventure segment up 5.0%. Cost per reached participant is low, clips double as safety reassurance for nervous first-timers, and results are measurable through online bookings with the 25-minute average lead time filling zipline slots.

Recommendation: BAC should choose social media influencer marketing. It targets the precise high-intent outdoor audience at a fraction of TV's cost, outperforms fair-day sponsorship in reach and continuity, and converts interest into the fast online bookings that fill scan times on the zipline. Regional TV is rejected as untargeted and unaffordable for a 28-person partnership; event sponsorship is rejected as valuable but too narrow and seasonal — BAC should run one launch-day fair as a supporting tactic, not the core strategy.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of BAC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of BAC with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and event sponsorship are rejected.

questions.question_text: BAC's seasonal labour turnover of 19% threatens guide quality at the new centre. Explain two benefits for BAC of using democratic leadership to improve motivation among its guides.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership lets guides help shape rotas, safety briefings and zipline loading routines, satisfying social and esteem needs (Maslow) and raising commitment. Involving guides in decisions about the zipline and climbing centre — as Tom and Ines already involve them — makes work meaningful and directly reduces the 19% off-peak turnover, keeping certified, gorge-experienced staff on payroll when spring visitors return and the 6,800-visitor quarter resumes.

Point 2: Involvement surfaces safety and service improvements from the people supervising 3,150 zipline descents a quarter, reinforcing the 4.7-star satisfaction score and the 0.6% equipment defect discipline. Motivated guides also refer friends into the spring intake, cutting recruitment costs, and the flat structure keeps communication fast and informal so concerns about rotas, certificates or fatigue surface before they become resignations — vital when a third of the summer team were hired cover for the climbing-centre season. Herzberg's recognition motivators reinforce this: guides who help set safety standards feel genuine ownership of every descent sold.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to BAC's turnover, safety culture and seasonality.

questions.question_text: BAC must recertify 7 of 28 guides in advanced swift-water rescue. Consider on-the-job coaching by lead guides or off-the-job recertification at the regional centre. Which should BAC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job coaching: Coaching by lead guides during live sessions costs nothing in fees, keeps all 7 guides on rota through the visitor season (protecting 2,400 climbing sessions and rafting trips), and is tailored to Bracken Gorge's specific rapids and load points. However, it carries no formal certification, so insurers, schools and auditors may reject it for swift-water compliance, and trainees on live trips in fast water create a real safety risk if under-qualified.

Off-the-job recertification: The regional centre course at $600 per guide — $4,200 for 7 guides — takes 2 days and yields recognised certification, satisfying insurers and schools booking rafting and updating rescue knowledge beyond in-house habits. It removes 7 of 28 guides for 2 days each, tightening the summer rota, and the content may not mirror Bracken Gorge's exact flow conditions without a follow-up site session.

Decision: BAC should choose off-the-job recertification at the regional centre. Swift-water rescue is a life-safety discipline where formal accreditation — not informal coaching — is what insurers, schools and auditors require; at only $4,200 it is cheap risk insurance against a catastrophic incident, and 2 days per guide is manageable even in peak months if staggered around the 2,400 climbing sessions and school-party bookings and the two lighter shoulder weeks. On-the-job coaching is rejected as the primary route because it cannot deliver recognised certification for a water-safety role; BAC should use lead-guide coaching only as consolidation after the course, and keep it for routine skills refreshers before each season's first rafting trip.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to BAC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of BAC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of BAC with a well-justified decision covering cost, safety and certification.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how BAC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $126,000 ÷ ($33 − $18) = $126,000 ÷ $15 = 8,400 units. Answer: break-even output is 8,400 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $33 − $18 = $15.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $15.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways BAC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. BAC's management can compare the 8,400-unit break-even output with actual output of 14,000 units to confirm the plan clears it comfortably, with a margin of safety of 5,600 units — tight enough to matter in off-peak months when turnover reaches 19%.
2. Contribution per unit of $15 lets BAC model group discounts: a $3 booking incentive takes price to $30 and contribution to $12, and managers can test whether extra rafting groups still cover fixed costs of $126,000.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $126,000 and contribution per unit helps management check the $400,000 bank loan repayments remain serviceable through the quiet season without leaning further on the $240,000 partners' capital.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($126,000 ÷ 14,000 units + $18 = $27.00 a unit) to benchmark trip profitability, price zipline versus rafting bundles, and target fuel or consumable waste within the $18 variable cost.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 8,400 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $15 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety (5,600 units) flags off-peak risk on 14,000 units; contribution modelling supports group discounting; fixed-cost cover tests the $400,000 bank loan against $126,000 fixed costs; and $27.00 unit cost informs bundle pricing and cost control across the season from Bracken Gorge.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate BAC's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has BAC's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.63 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.82 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.00 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.14 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $60,000 inventories + $25,000 trade receivables + $70,000 cash = $155,000; 2025 current assets = $75,000 + $30,000 + $95,000 = $200,000. 2024 = $155,000 ÷ $95,000 = 1.63 : 1; 2025 = $200,000 ÷ $110,000 = 1.82 : 1. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($155,000 − $60,000) ÷ $95,000 = $95,000 ÷ $95,000 = 1.00 : 1; 2025 = ($200,000 − $75,000) ÷ $110,000 = $125,000 ÷ $110,000 = 1.14 : 1.

Evaluation: Liquidity improved markedly. Cash rose from $70,000 to $95,000 while trade receivables stayed tiny ($25,000 to $30,000 — walk-ins and online pre-payment, a structural strength for an activity operator collecting at booking). Inventories rose only modestly to $75,000 as equipment and stock were built ahead of the new centre; current liabilities rose 16% to $110,000 as BAC used supplier credit during the build. The inventory-excluded measure cleared 1.00 to 1.14, meaning even stripping out safety stock BAC could meet short-term debts — a crucial buffer while $640,000 of construction is underway and $400,000 of bank debt is serviced. Capital employed rose to $1,360,000 and non-current assets to $1,250,000, consistent with the build programme.

Conclusion: BAC's financial position has clearly improved on both measures, and the improvement does not rely on inventory. The main residual risk is seasonal cash flow in the quiet months rather than year-round solvency — BAC should stagger supplier payments and hold a dedicated off-peak cash fund so the stronger position survives until the zipline centre opens and the 6,300-visitor growth trend continues.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether BAC's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for BAC of becoming an eco-certified adventure operator.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Eco-certification differentiates BAC in the outdoor-leisure market growing 6.3%, strengthening trust with schools, families and insurers booking the zipline centre — vital for a safety-critical business whose 900 feedback forms already average 4.7 out of 5. It supports premium pricing on guided trips, positions BAC ahead of rivals as domestic adventure-tourism visits rise 5.0%, and can reduce fuel and consumable waste within the $18 variable cost.

Disadvantage: Certification demands audits, documented procedures and staff retraining — recurring administrative cost for a 28-person partnership carrying a $400,000 bank loan and $126,000 of fixed costs. If swift-water and site practices slip during construction, failed audits would damage credibility just as BAC needs school and corporate contracts; the 7-guide certification gap shows compliance capacity is already stretched, so BAC must fund training (2 days per guide) before promoting the badge, and budget for annual recertification and audit fees on top of the $600 per-guide cost — a recurring commitment the partnership should schedule against quiet-season cash flow.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to BAC's market, costs and safety obligations.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 5.1% minimum wage increase and the 10.2% rise in fuel and transport costs will affect BAC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): BAC's $400,000 bank loan costs roughly $3,000 a year more (0.75% on $400,000) — modest against $126,000 fixed costs and the $640,000 total investment. Higher rates may dampen discretionary outdoor spending, though Bracken Gorge sessions (3,150 zipline descents last quarter) are destination activities that are less rate-sensitive than big-ticket household purchases.

Minimum wage increase (5.1%, to $11.98): Front-desk, base and junior roles sit near the minimum; certified swift-water guides requiring $600 recertification command above-minimum pay. If, for illustration, 12 of the 28 staff are near the minimum, the extra $0.58 per hour costs about $13,900 a year — absorbable by the flat democratic team through rotas and the off-peak turnover savings of 19%.

Fuel and transport costs (+10.2%): BAC shuttles clients between the gorge car park, jump-off point and rafting put-ins daily; fuel is structural to the $18 unit cost on every one of 14,000 units. If, for illustration, transport and fuel represent about a third of the unit cost ($6), a 10.2% rise adds about $0.61 per unit — roughly $8,500 a year — recurring, unavoidable and likely to drift upward with safety-equipment inflation (+7.4%).

Conclusion: The 10.2% rise in fuel and transport costs will have the greatest impact. Unlike the interest rise (about $3,000 a year) it hits every unit, every day, and unlike the wage rise it applies to the entire 14,000-unit volume rather than a subset of entry-level roles — and BAC cannot quietly reprice mid-season without deterring the outdoor-leisure segment growing 6.3%. The wage rise is second; interest is smallest and hedgeable when the loan is refinanced. BAC should consolidate shuttle runs, negotiate fuel contracts, and bundle transport into premium adventure packages to defend the $15 contribution per unit.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to BAC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on BAC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of BAC with a well-justified judgement that the fuel and transport cost rise has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
